get.description:
Protected Resource Metadata (RFC 9728) — per-tenant payload.

Group 7 of the multi-tenant subdomain routing change:

  - ``resource`` is the per-tenant URL, read from
    ``request.state.resource_uri`` set by
    ``TenantResolutionMiddleware`` upstream.
  - ``authorization_servers`` is a one-element array containing
    the singleton AS issuer URL identifier (per RFC 9728 §2 —
    the issuer URL, NOT the metadata document URL).
  - Only fields defined by RFC 9728 are emitted. No vendor-
    specific hints (no ``application``, no ``client_id_hint``).
    Per-tenant routing inside the AS happens via ``client_id``
    carried in the authorize request — operators get the
    per-tenant ``client_id`` from
    ``GET /api/v1/admin/tenants/{id}/connector-config`` and paste
    it into Claude Web's "Advanced OAuth" settings (D19).
  - ``Vary: Host`` is emitted on every response so intermediate
    caches do not serve one tenant's payload to another.

Subpath form (``/.well-known/oauth-protected-resource/{path}``)
accepts ``mcp-remote`` and clients that fetch with a path
component. Same response shape; the ``path`` arg is unused.

Failure modes:
  - Tenant not resolved (no ``request.state.resource_uri``): the
    client probably bypassed ``TenantResolutionMiddleware`` (or
    hit a path that doesn't have one). Returns 404 — the
    operator-facing answer is "this URL doesn't host PRM."
  - OAuth not configured (no ``OIDC_ISSUER_URL``): returns 404
    with a parseable OAuth error so MCP clients render a useful
    message.

post.description:
Dynamic Client Registration (RFC 7591) — DISABLED.

Returns HTTP 405 Method Not Allowed with a hint pointing at the
connector-config admin endpoint. Per design.md D16 + Group 7,
DCR is intentionally disabled in this change — the per-tenant
Casdoor apps carry ``dcrPolicy: disabled`` and operators are
expected to use ``GET /api/v1/admin/tenants/{id}/connector-config``
to retrieve a pre-provisioned ``client_id`` + ``client_secret``.
Enabling DCR per tenant is tracked as a separate follow-up
(B2 from #237 comments).

Tenant-resolved (so ``Vary: Host`` is emitted) but the body is
identical for every tenant — defensive cache safety.

405.description: DCR is disabled; use connector-config instead.

Requires admin authentication via Depends(require_permission) — same

Probe the upload-feature infrastructure (S3 + DuckDB).

Returns ``200`` when either: uploads are disabled, or all configured
subsystems (S3, DuckDB) report ``connected``. Returns ``503`` when a
configured subsystem is unreachable — this is the signal operators
need to distinguish "feature off" from "feature on but broken" that
the readiness probe deliberately avoids (readiness is scoped to
metadata DB to keep its latency predictable).

post.description:
Write one ``login`` or ``login_failed`` event for the asserted acting user.

A user's own token records its login in the auth middleware; an app that
forwards a shared key never sends one, so it reports the sign-in here.
Wrong passwords never reach the app; the identity provider holds those.
``tenant_id`` may be the tenant's id or slug; the row stores the id, so it
shows in that tenant's scoped log. 503 when the event was not saved, so
the caller knows the sign-in went unrecorded.

post.description:
Rotate the encryption key for data source secrets.

Key rotation requires the server to be restarted with both old and new
encryption keys configured. This endpoint is a placeholder — the full
implementation requires a deployment workflow that provides access to
both keys simultaneously.

Steps (manual for now):
1. Generate a new Fernet key.
2. Set ``DATA_SOURCE_ENCRYPTION_KEY_NEW`` in environment.
3. Redeploy the server.
4. Call this endpoint to re-encrypt all secrets with the new key.
5. Remove the old key and set the new key as ``DATA_SOURCE_ENCRYPTION_KEY``.

501.description: Key rotation status

access token at all (the refresh path clears it while keeping tenant/user), so
a user-only read would strand the flow.

Widening it grants no new authority: a ``chat-service`` key already holds the
full grant lifecycle for ANY server in its tenant (upsert / evict / refresh
lease), and ``auth_config`` crosses the wire as KEK ciphertext this service
cannot decrypt — the key never leaves xfalcon-web. A service principal reads
under ``app.role='service'`` (``mcp_servers_service_role_all``); a user
principal stays owner-scoped, so no tenant member gains visibility it lacked.

post.summary: Record an MCP server's observed health status (status only; user OR service principal)
post.description:
Record an observed health outcome: ``status`` plus a reason and a fresh
``last_health_check``, in ONE write.

BOTH outcomes in one call, deliberately. This endpoint used to hardcode
``status='error'``, so a caller reporting a SUCCESSFUL discovery had to mark the
server faulted and then correct it through the general
``PATCH /mcp-servers/{id}``. That is a two-write sequence with a window in which
a healthy server is durably errored, and a failure of the second write left the
row ``status='error'`` carrying a success message permanently. It also
contradicted the reason this endpoint exists: the general PATCH can rewrite
``url`` / ``auth_type`` / ``auth_config``, so routing any status write through it
is exactly the credential-surface widening the narrow endpoint was created to
avoid. Accepting the target status here removes the need for the PATCH on the
status path entirely.

Accepts BOTH principal kinds on purpose. The web engine reaches this from two
caller classes: an interactive turn (user bearer available) and a token-less
run — headless report-refresh, first-class API-key, internal approval-resume —
which has no Casdoor token to present and so must come in on a chat-service
key. Refusing the service principal here is what previously forced that write
to stay on direct Postgres.

A service principal writes under ``app.role='service'`` (admitted by
``mcp_servers_service_role_all``); a user principal writes under its own GUCs
(owner-scoped ``mcp_servers_update_own``), so a member can still only restatus a
server it owns. Neither path can reach any column outside the status triple —
see :class:`McpServerStatusReport`.

Flip a server to ``status='error'`` with a reason and a health timestamp.

Identical to ``:set-status`` with ``status='error'`` — same implementation, same
principal rules, same column set. Kept so callers written against the
fault-only endpoint keep working; they should move to ``:set-status``, which can
also report a healthy outcome without a second write.

put.summary: Replace a server's advertised tool set, and optionally stamp its health status, in one transaction (user OR service)
put.description:
Persist the result of a completed MCP discovery handshake.

The caller performs the handshake (it holds the KEK that decrypts
``auth_config``) and posts the resulting set here; this endpoint owns the
database half. See :class:`McpToolReconcile` for why the split falls exactly
on the credential boundary, and why an empty ``tools`` list is honoured rather
than treated as a no-op.

Both principal kinds are accepted for the same reason as ``:set-status``: the
OAuth-callback and user-Refresh paths carry a user bearer, while a token-less
run reaches discovery with only a chat-service key.

``tenant_id`` on inserted rows is taken from the SERVER row, not the request
body and not the principal — the tools belong to whoever owns the server, and
a service principal has no user tenant of its own to inherit from. The server
is resolved under the caller's own GUCs first, so a user principal can only
reconcile a server RLS already lets it see.

Pass ``status_message`` to stamp the server ``connected`` in this SAME
transaction and skip the follow-up ``:set-status`` call entirely. Discovery
then costs the caller ONE round trip instead of two, and — more importantly
— the catalog and the health status can no longer disagree: previously the
reconcile could commit and the status write fail, leaving a server stuck on
``connecting`` while advertising a freshly-populated tool list.

Requires the ``mcp_tools_server_id_name_key`` unique constraint to exist —
it is the ``ON CONFLICT`` arbiter below. A database where that constraint
was skipped (see the UNIQUE block in 04_constraints.sql for how that
happens) fails EVERY call here with SQLSTATE 42P10.

get.summary: Resolve the shared OAuth grant for a server (service-context, tenant-scoped)
get.description:
Read the shared per-server grant for the web tier's refresh flow.

Service-context + tenant-scoped (never owner-scoped): the owner-scoped
app-role SELECT policy would hide a grant whose ``granted_by_user_id`` is
another member or NULL, so the web fast-path (return the cached access token
without acquiring a lease) could never see it. The returned token columns are
opaque ciphertext — useless without the web-side KEK — and per-server access
is authorized upstream, so returning them to a tenant-bound principal matches
the direct path exactly.

put.summary: Upsert the shared OAuth grant for a server (service-context, tenant-scoped)
put.description:
Persist the tokens the web OAuth callback minted for ``server_id``.

Mirrors the direct callback UPSERT: one shared grant per server
(``server_id`` is UNIQUE), keyed by the path parameter and written under the
service role (grant writes are RLS service-only). The server must belong to
the caller's tenant — verified here exactly as the callback verifies the
server/tenant pair before persisting — so a caller cannot mint or clobber a
grant for another tenant's server (a server outside the tenant is
indistinguishable from a missing one → ``not_found``). ``refresh_version`` is
bumped ATOMICALLY in one statement (0 on first mint, +1 on every re-mint so
any in-flight version-pinned refresh CAS fails and re-reads the fresh
tokens), closing the read-modify-write race the direct path carried.
``granted_by_user_id`` stays NULL (audit-lineage only). Token columns are
opaque ciphertext (the KEK never leaves the web tier).

delete.summary: Evict the shared OAuth grant for a server (idempotent, tenant-scoped)
delete.description:

(reauth required). Service-context + tenant-scoped, and IDEMPOTENT: evicting
a grant that is already gone returns ``deleted=False`` with 200 — never a
404 — matching the direct path's best-effort eviction (a delete matching
zero rows is not an error).

put.summary: Replace a provider key's credential with a newly submitted cleartext secret
put.description:
Re-seal the row's credential from cleartext, taking ownership of it.

Idempotent in the REST sense — submitting the same secret twice leaves the
same credential stored (the ciphertext differs, because the nonce does).

Also the migration path off a client-side envelope: a client that can still
open its own legacy ``enc:v1`` / ``xfdc:v1`` row submits the plaintext here
once, and the row becomes readable from every other client of that user. The
envelope marker is merged over whatever the row carried, so a migrated row
stops claiming a client owns it while the caller's own metadata keys survive.

post.summary: Return a provider key's credential in cleartext to its owner
post.description:
Decrypt one provider credential for its owner.

POST, not GET, deliberately: the response body is a secret, so it must not be
a URL a browser history, proxy log, or referrer header can name, and must not
be revalidated from a cache. ``no-store`` says the same thing to every hop.

Two callers, one row scoping. A JWT user resolves their own credential and
sends no body. A ``chat-service`` principal resolves a NAMED user's
credential — the path a server tier needs when it must serve a request with a
user's provider key but holds no JWT for that user (web's
``/v1/chat/completions``, whose own caller authenticates with a first-class
``xf_chat`` key that is refused here). Either way the tenant comes from the
authenticated principal and never the body, so a service credential cannot
reach across tenants.

Ownership is enforced by the DATABASE, not by a check here: the read runs
under ``app.tenant_id`` / ``app.user_id`` set to the pair being resolved, with
``app.role`` unset, so ``provider_keys_manage_own`` applies and a row
belonging to anyone else is simply invisible. That is why the service path
needs no new RLS policy — it borrows the owner's context rather than
bypassing it.

A row whose credential this service cannot read answers ``conflict``, whether
because the envelope is a client's or because it is ours but was sealed for a
different owner or secret class. Reporting it as anything vaguer would invite
the caller to retry; the actionable step is to re-submit the secret to
``PUT /provider-keys/{id}/secret``.

Accepts BOTH user (Casdoor JWT) and service (chat-service key) principals —

ATTRIBUTION. ``user_id`` is NOT NULL, and a service principal has no user of
its own, so it would otherwise record the ``audit_actor`` sentinel — which
erases WHO performed a privileged act, the single most useful field in a
security trail. A service principal may therefore supply ``actor_user_id``:
the human it is acting on behalf of, taken from the caller's own verified
session and stamped into ``user_id`` so the actor stays in the indexed NOT NULL
column instead of a jsonb key.

That is a web-tier attestation rather than a data-plane-verified one, and the
trade is deliberate: the alternative (letting users write privileged actions
directly) would make the row NAMED but FORGEABLE. Service-only authorship plus
a declared actor keeps it both unforgeable by tenant members and attributable.
A user principal supplying ``actor_user_id`` is rejected — its own id is
already authoritative, so an override could only ever be an impersonation
attempt.

ApiKeyUpdate.title: ApiKeyUpdate
ApiKeyUpdate.description:
Partial update. Only fields explicitly present in the body are applied
(``model_fields_set``), so an omitted field is left untouched.

Two rules make revocation an unambiguous, one-way audit fact:

* **Revocation is terminal.** ``revoked_at: null`` is rejected — a retired
  credential must never be resurrected through a partial update. (Omitting
  ``revoked_at`` is the way to leave it alone; only an *explicit* null is
  an error.) Re-sending a ``revoked_at`` for an already-revoked key is
  accepted and idempotent, but the originally recorded instant is kept.
* **Revocation is exclusive.** When ``revoked_at`` is present it must be
  the only field in the request. Re-scoping or renaming a key in the same
  call that retires it collapses two decisions into one audit row whose
  meaning cannot be reconstructed afterwards.

Per-tenant connector configuration payload.

``server_url`` + ``mcp_url`` (derived from the tenant's slug + the
server's ``MCP_BASE_HOST`` / ``MCP_PUBLIC_SCHEME`` / ``MCP_PUBLIC_PORT``),
the OIDC issuer + decrypted Casdoor credentials, and the rendered
``redirect_uris[]`` allowlist.

The ``claude_connector_setup`` block is a human-readable instruction
fragment surfaced in dashboard tooltips so operators don't have to
re-derive the D19 "one Claude custom connector per tenant URL" rule
from the docs every time.

The endpoint sets ``Cache-Control: no-store, private`` (per task
9.6) so this payload — which contains the decrypted ``client_secret``
— never lands in any cache. The encrypted secret is decrypted only
on each call.

McpServerStatusReport.title: McpServerStatusReport
McpServerStatusReport.description:
Record an OBSERVED health outcome for a server. Status-only, by construction.

This exists INSTEAD of widening :class:`McpServerUpdate` to service principals.
A status write is the one mcp_servers mutation a token-less caller must make (a
headless or API-key run whose MCP server dies mid-turn — or whose discovery
handshake succeeds — has no user bearer to present), but ``McpServerUpdate`` can
rewrite ``url``, ``auth_type`` and ``auth_config``: admitting a service key
there would hand every tenant's connection targets and credential envelopes a
write path in order to buy a status flag. The fields here are the complete set
the status path touches, so least privilege is a property of the SCHEMA rather
than a convention a future handler edit could quietly break.

``status`` IS THE FIX FOR A REAL CORRUPTION, not a convenience. The endpoint
used to hardcode ``'error'``, so a caller reporting SUCCESS had to mark the
server faulted first and then correct it with a second, independent
``PATCH /mcp-servers/{id}``. That left a window in which a perfectly healthy
server was durably ``status='error'``, and if the second call failed the row
stayed errored carrying a SUCCESS message (``"12 tools discovered"``) forever
while the caller reported ok. Widening the status — and ONLY the status — closes
the window in one call without reopening the credential surface: the narrowness,
not the hardcoded value, is what makes a service key safe here.

McpToolReconcile.title: McpToolReconcile
McpToolReconcile.description:
The full tool set a server currently advertises — a SET, not a patch.

WHY THIS IS PERSIST-ONLY, AND WHY THE HANDSHAKE STAYS IN THE CALLER.
Discovery has two halves: an outbound ``initialize`` + ``tools/list`` against
the operator's MCP endpoint, and the reconcile of the result into
``mcp_tools``. Only the second half can move here. The first needs the
server's decrypted ``auth_config``, and the KEK that decrypts it never leaves
xfalcon-web by design (see this module's header) — so a data-plane handshake
would require replicating every tenant's MCP credentials into a second
service. Splitting at the credential boundary keeps that invariant and still
removes the caller's need for a database handle, which is what the direct-DB
cutover was actually blocked on.

``tools`` is authoritative and REPLACES the server's set: names absent from
it are deleted (the server withdrew them), names present are upserted on
``mcp_tools_server_id_name_key``. Both halves run in ONE transaction, so a
reconcile can never leave a server advertising a partially-updated catalog.

An EMPTY list is meaningful and honoured — a server that legitimately
advertises nothing deletes all its tools. Callers must therefore send this
only after a SUCCESSFUL handshake; on a failed probe, record the fault instead
(``POST /mcp-servers/{id}:set-status`` with ``status='error'``) and leave the
catalog alone, or a transient outage silently strips every tool the user had.

MessageSearchPage.title: MessageSearchPage
MessageSearchPage.description:
``CursorPage[ChatMessage]`` plus the match strategy the server APPLIED.

Additive over the plain page envelope: ``items``/``next_cursor``/``has_more``/
``limit`` are inherited unchanged, so a consumer that ignores the new field
reads exactly the same body as before.

``applied_mode`` exists because ``mode`` is a query PARAMETER on a
pre-existing endpoint, and FastAPI ignores unrecognised query parameters
instead of rejecting them. Against a deployment that predates ``mode``,
``mode=substring`` is therefore dropped silently, the server re-runs the FTS
query the caller has already established returned nothing, and the caller
receives an empty page with no 4xx/5xx anywhere — a capability regression that
is indistinguishable from a genuine empty match set. Echoing the applied
strategy makes that skew detectable: an OLD server omits the field entirely,
which is the signal a caller asserts on (see the field description).

``secret`` is the cleartext credential; this service encrypts it before the
write and marks the row as its own. That is the path every client should
use — it is what lets one credential entered on the web app work in the
desktop app and back, because no client-held key material is involved.

``api_key`` is the legacy path: ciphertext a client sealed with its own KEK,
stored opaque. It exists only while xfalcon-web and xfalcon-desktop (which
deploy separately from this service) still seal client-side, and is removed
once both have cut over. Rows created this way cannot be resolved here.

``x-run-id`` and used to register the in-process abort controller + SSE stream
before the row exists), so the caller may supply it. When omitted the server
generates one. Re-POSTing an existing id is idempotent (returns the existing
run) rather than a duplicate.

RunFinalize.title: RunFinalize
RunFinalize.description:
Atomically finalize a run: persist the assistant message, bump the
conversation, upsert budget usage (SAVEPOINT-fenced), and set the terminal
status. Mirrors web ``finalizeRunCompletion``.

``expected_from`` is the SAME compare-and-set predicate
:class:`RunStatusUpdate` carries, with the same shape (a single status or a
list) and the same default (force only while the run is still non-terminal —
first-terminal-writer wins). A fenced miss is a 409, not a silent no-op.

It is not optional polish. Without it the finalize's run UPDATE was
``WHERE id = $1`` alone, so a plain Stop-button race durably corrupted the
record: the cancel route writes ``status='cancelled'`` + ``completed_at`` +
``metadata.termination_reason='user_cancel'``, then the engine's in-flight
finalize — which correctly SKIPS the assistant-message insert on seeing the
terminal status — overwrote the row with ``status='completed'`` and the
completion metadata anyway. The durable result was a run reporting
``completed`` whose answer existed only in ``runs.output_message`` with no
``chat_messages`` row (the conversation lost its reply on reload) and whose
cancel had been erased, while the client was told ``run.cancel``. The
predicate makes the first terminal writer's ``status``, ``completed_at`` AND
``metadata`` survive intact.

RunFinalizeResult.title: RunFinalizeResult

id/sequence (null when ``content`` was empty and no message was written).

RunProgressUpdate.title: RunProgressUpdate

without touching its status.

RunStatusUpdate.title: RunStatusUpdate
RunStatusUpdate.description:
Transition a run's status.

``expected_from`` is an optional compare-and-set predicate: the update only
lands if the run is currently in one of the given statuses
(first-terminal-writer wins). With no ``expected_from`` the transition is
forced only while the run is still non-terminal. The optional columns are
set atomically with the status flip.

It accepts a LIST as well as a single status. A single string was enough for
every terminal transition, but the engine's ordinary streaming path issues
``['queued', 'running']`` — one write that must land from either state
without caring which. A scalar-only predicate cannot express that, so the
web tier fell back to a direct Postgres UPDATE on the main path of every
run: not an edge case, the common one, and invisible because it looked like
a normal CAS guard rather than a missing capability.

A bare string stays valid and is treated as a one-element list, so every
existing caller and the published contract shape are unaffected.

TruncateRequest.title: TruncateRequest
TruncateRequest.description:
Destructively truncate a conversation at/after ``from_message_id``.

``from_message_id`` is the cutoff: that message and everything after it (its
tool_calls, artifacts, attachments, and trailing runs) is hard-deleted. The
web layer resolves *which* message is the cutoff (its edit/regenerate
boundary) and calls this primitive; the primitive itself just truncates.

TruncateResult.title: TruncateResult
TruncateResult.description:
Outcome of an atomic *destructive* truncate — the hard-delete counterpart
of a soft rewind. Everything at/after the cutoff message is removed.

``freed_attachment_storage_keys`` are the storage keys of the cut messages'
attachments, captured before their rows were deleted so the caller can
reclaim the backing objects (the row was the only handle to the key).

decision. `target` and `target_type` are immutable — to change them,
delete and re-create.

change_note.title: Change Note
change_note.description: Why the edit is made. Stored on the new version (returned in the version history) and recorded on the memory.updated audit event

UpdateMemoryRequest.title: UpdateMemoryRequest
UpdateMemoryRequest.description:
Request body for PATCH /api/v1/admin/memories/{id}.

Content-bearing fields (content, title, category, tables, keywords) trigger
supersession — a new version row is inserted and the old one is ended.
`change_note` is stored on that new version and recorded on the audit event;
on its own it changes nothing and is rejected.

UpdateTenantRequest.title: UpdateTenantRequest
UpdateTenantRequest.description:
Update payload for ``PATCH /api/v1/admin/tenants/{id}``.

``slug`` is deliberately NOT a declared field — slug rename is out
of scope of the multi-tenant-subdomain-routing change. The model
uses ``extra="allow"`` so unknown fields (including ``slug``) are
captured in ``body.model_extra``; the handler inspects that and
rejects with HTTP 400 ("slug is immutable") rather than silently
dropping the field. No-default-422 surprise from ``extra="forbid"``
— operators get a clear actionable error.
